answer.label: Not William Butler Yeats — actually Plutarch (paraphrased)
answer.authorDates: c. 46 – c. 120 AD · Greek biographer, essayist & Middle Platonist philosopher
answer.sourceLine: There is no trace of this sentence in Yeats's Collected Works, his collected letters, or major quotation dictionaries. Quote Investigator traces the underlying idea to Plutarch's essay on listening — though the exact “pail and fire” wording is a modern paraphrase that first appears in print in 1968, already credited there to Plutarch, and was only reassigned to Yeats later, by 1987.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “On Listening to Lectures” (De Auditu / De Recta Ratione Audiendi), an essay in Plutarch's Moralia
Frank Cole Babbitt, Loeb Classical Library 197, Harvard University Press, 1927
1968, in James Johnson Sweeney's Vision and Image: A Way of Seeing (there credited to Plutarch, not Yeats)

source.excerpt: For the mind does not require filling like a bottle, but rather, like wood, it only requires kindling to create in it an impulse to think independently and an ardent desire for the truth.
trail: No occurrence of this line turns up in Yeats's Collected Works, his collected letters, the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, or Bartlett's Familiar Quotations — researcher Robert Strong found “no pail, no fire” in any of them, as detailed in his investigation ↗.

The underlying idea traces to Plutarch's essay “On Listening to Lectures,” where he writes that the mind “does not require filling like a bottle, but rather, like wood, it only requires kindling” — see the 1927 Loeb translation ↗.

The exact “pail” and “fire” wording first appears in print in 1968, in James Johnson Sweeney's Vision and Image: A Way of Seeing — already attributed there to Plutarch, not Yeats, per Quote Investigator's chronology ↗.

By 1987 the Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations had reassigned the same line to Yeats, likely because Sweeney's book placed the Plutarch paraphrase directly beside a genuine Yeats quotation — a mix-up documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: This 1927 translation is the closest confirmed primary-source wording. The popular “pail”/“fire” phrasing quoted everywhere online is a later paraphrase, not Plutarch's own words.

artifact.linkText: Plutarch, De Auditu (On Listening to Lectures)

source.rightsNote: The familiar “pail” and “fire” wording is a paraphrase of Plutarch's Greek that first appears in print in 1968 with no identified author, so no responsible copyright status can be assigned to that exact phrasing. Plutarch's own 1st-century text (and the 1927 Loeb translation of it) is long in the public domain, but that translation reads “bottle” and “wood,” not “pail” and “fire.”

author.name: Plutarch
author.heading: About Plutarch
author.metaLine: c. 46 – c. 120 AD · Greek biographer, essayist & Middle Platonist philosopher
author.bio: Plutarch of Chaeronea was a Greek biographer and essayist best known for his Parallel Lives and the sprawling essay collection Moralia. In his essay “On Listening to Lectures,” addressed to a young student beginning his philosophical education, he argued that a mind is not a vessel to be filled but wood waiting to be kindled — the germ of the idea now popularly, but wrongly, credited to Yeats.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This saying is one of the most widely repeated fake quotes in education circles, and its trail runs through more than one misattribution.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in Yeats's Collected Works, his collected letters, the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, or Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, per Robert Strong's investigation in “Advice on Lighting Fires” ↗.

A 1966 citation in the Malaysian Journal of Education attaches a near-identical “kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel” line to Socrates — another attribution Quote Investigator found no evidence for, per its origin research ↗.

items.who: James Johnson Sweeney's 1968 book Vision and Image: A Way of Seeing
items.why: It placed a Plutarch paraphrase directly beside a genuine Yeats quotation; later compilers, including the 1987 Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations, appear to have transferred the ascription to Yeats, as traced by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The closest real source is Plutarch's essay “On Listening to Lectures,” which argues the mind “does not require filling like a bottle, but rather, like wood, it only requires kindling” — the idea behind the modern saying, even though the crisp “pail and fire” phrasing was coined by an unidentified paraphraser no earlier than 1968; see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this fake quote won't die
lead: Few education slogans travel farther than this one — commencement speeches, teacher-training slides, and social media routinely credit it to Yeats, presumably because a famous poet's name makes the pedagogy sound more inspired. But it is one of the internet's most durable fake quotes: no researcher has ever located it in anything Yeats wrote, said, or was recorded saying.

The paper trail instead leads back nearly two thousand years to Plutarch, who argued in his essay “On Listening to Lectures” that a student's mind is not a jar to be filled but wood waiting to be kindled. The crisp, modern “pail and fire” phrasing itself, though, only shows up in print starting in 1968 — already one step removed from Plutarch's actual words, and misattributed to Yeats less than twenty years after that.
context.pull: No researcher has ever located this sentence in anything Yeats wrote, said, or was recorded saying.
